title: Two dreams in a cell
hookLine: two prisoners ask about their dreams, and Yusuf first speaks to them of the One

cards: A hospital ward, a barracks, a long night shift: in hard places, people find each other. They trade stories. They ask the questions they'd never ask at home.
Two young men go into prison with Yusuf. The Qur'an says they'd noticed something about him: we see you're one of those who do good. And each of them brings him a dream.
The first says: I saw myself pressing grapes for wine. The second says: I saw myself carrying bread on my head, and birds were eating from it. Tell us what it means.

teach.b: Surah Yusuf. Yusuf has the answer, and he makes them wait, not to be clever, but because he has something to give them first. He says: before your next meal arrives, I'll tell you.
This is part of what my Lord has taught me. Then he tells them who he is: I follow the way of my fathers, Ibrahim, Ishaq and Ya'qub.
There's Ibrahim again, who looked at the stars and loved what doesn't set, weeks ago on this path.

teach.h: MY TWO COMPANIONS OF THE PRISON.
teach.b: Then Yusuf speaks to them tenderly: ya sahibayi s-sijn, my two companions of the prison. Not you criminals. Not you poor souls.
Companions. And he asks them: many separate lords, or Allah, the One, the Overwhelming? The decision, he says, belongs to Allah alone.
That's the heart of it for Yusuf.
Before their future, the One. Then he answers, straight. One of you will pour wine for his master again.
The other will be crucified, and birds will eat from his head. The matter you asked about is decided. It isn't gentle, but it's honest.
To the one he knew would be freed, Yusuf says: mention me to your master.

The verse says Satan made him forget, so Yusuf stayed in prison a few more years. The Qur'an's word for that stretch is bid', a handful. It doesn't give the number; commentators usually explain it as three to nine.
Some good you do, the world forgets for years.

how: Muslims often cite Yusuf in prison as a model of da'wa, sharing faith with kindness and honesty; his address "my two companions of the prison" is quoted as an example of gentle speech.

o: a whole lifetime spent behind prison walls
a single season, from one harvest to the next
a handful: a few years, the number not given

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: bread on his head, birds eating
my two companions of the prison

s: Yusuf answered the dreams before anything else
he spoke first of his fathers' way and of the One, then answered.
ya sahibayi s-sijn: my two companions of the prison.
the Qur'an says exactly how many years Yusuf stayed in prison
it says bid' sinin, a handful of years, usually explained as three to nine.

games.q: you're Yusuf. two cellmates bring you their dreams and ask what they mean. you know the answers. what do you do first?
o: tell them the meanings right away.
speak to them of the One, then tell them.
tell only the one with the good news.
games.why: he tells them the answer is coming before their next meal, then speaks of his fathers' way and of Allah, the One. only then does he interpret.

practice: Yusuf gave his cellmates something before they got what they came for.

Think of someone sharing a hard place with you right now, a coworker on the same long project, a family member in the same waiting room, a classmate in the same impossible course, and what you could give them before they ask: a word of encouragement, a coffee, a sincere compliment, calling them companion in your own way.
If you pray, you can ask to be good company.

wordCard.voice: Bid', a handful: the Qur'an's word for the few more years Yusuf stayed in prison after the cupbearer forgot to mention him.

orig.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 12:39 and 12:41: "O my two companions of the prison."

carryVoice: Your line: start with the one. Even in a cell, that came first. That's day sixty-four.
